Blackjack Side Bets Explained: Why Perfect Pairs and 21+3 Carry a Much Higher House Edge

Published September 1, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Sit down at almost any blackjack table, physical or online, and you'll see a small circle or box next to the main betting spot labeled Perfect Pairs, 21+3, or something similar, usually promising a payout far bigger than anything the main hand can pay. It's an easy add-on: same deal, same cards, one extra chip. What the felt doesn't advertise is that the math behind that extra circle has almost nothing in common with the hand you're actually there to play, and the gap between the two is bigger than most players realize until they see it laid out.

What a blackjack side bet actually is

A side bet is a separate wager placed alongside your main blackjack hand, settled on its own rules using cards you're already being dealt anyway. It doesn't affect how the main hand is played and it doesn't require you to change any of your basic-strategy decisions — you place the extra chip before the cards come out, the dealer resolves it immediately once your first two cards (and sometimes the dealer's up card) are visible, and then the main hand plays out completely independently. That independence is part of the appeal: it feels like a free-standing lottery ticket bolted onto a game you already understand.

The two most common side bets at US casinos and online blackjack tables are Perfect Pairs and 21+3, though variations exist under names like Lucky Ladies, Bust It, and Royal Match, each built around a different way of scoring the same handful of cards.

Perfect Pairs: betting on your own first two cards

Perfect Pairs pays out if your first two cards form a pair, with the payout scaled to how specific a pair it is. A standard paytable looks roughly like this:

OutcomeExampleTypical payout
Mixed pair7 of hearts, 7 of clubs (same rank, different color)5 to 1
Colored pair7 of hearts, 7 of diamonds (same rank, same color, different suit)10 to 1
Perfect pair7 of hearts, 7 of hearts (same rank and exact suit, from a multi-deck shoe)25 to 1

Because most tables deal from a six- or eight-deck shoe, a "perfect" pair (identical rank and suit) is possible — the second 7 of hearts is simply a different physical card from another deck in the shoe. The rarer the exact match, the higher the payout, which is the same basic design principle behind long-shot bets across the casino floor: bigger prize, much lower hit frequency.

21+3: your hand plus the dealer's up card as a poker hand

21+3 combines your two starting cards with the dealer's single visible up card — three cards total — and pays out if they form a recognized three-card poker hand. A typical paytable rewards, in ascending order: a flush (three cards of the same suit, not sequential), a straight (three sequential ranks, mixed suits), three of a kind (matching rank, different suits), a straight flush (sequential and same suit), and suited trips (identical rank and suit, only possible from a multi-deck shoe) at the top. Payouts commonly range from around 5 to 1 for a straight up to 100 to 1 for suited trips, depending on the specific paytable a casino has chosen to run.

What makes 21+3 slightly different from Perfect Pairs is that its outcome depends partly on the dealer's card, which means the same two starting cards can settle as a loss or a win purely based on what the dealer happens to be showing — a detail that catches new players off guard the first time a strong-looking pair of suited cards misses simply because the dealer's up card doesn't complete anything.

Why the house edge runs so much higher than the main hand

Played with correct basic strategy, the main blackjack hand carries a house edge of roughly 0.5% at a typical six-deck table with standard rules — one of the lowest edges of any game on the casino floor. Side bets don't come close. Because they're paying out on rare, specific card combinations rather than a broad outcome like "beat the dealer's total," the house edge on a typical Perfect Pairs or 21+3 bet commonly runs somewhere in the 3% to 8% range, and some paytable variants run notably higher than that. There's also no strategy chart to lower it: unlike the main hand, where basic strategy is the entire reason the edge gets as low as it does, a side bet's outcome is fixed the moment the cards are dealt. There's no decision to make and nothing to optimize.

BetTypical house edgeCan strategy improve it?
Main hand, basic strategy~0.5%Yes — this is the entire point of basic strategy
Perfect PairsRoughly 3% to 11%, depending on paytableNo — outcome is fixed at the deal
21+3Roughly 3% to 8%, depending on paytableNo — outcome is fixed at the deal

Those ranges are wide because paytables genuinely differ meaningfully by casino and by which variant of a side bet is on the felt — always check the payout table printed on the table itself (or the game rules screen online) rather than assuming every "Perfect Pairs" table pays the same, since two versions with the same name can carry a noticeably different edge.

A worked example: 100 hands with and without a side bet

Say you're flat-betting $10 a hand on blackjack for 100 hands, playing correct basic strategy throughout. Your expected loss on the main hand alone, at a 0.5% house edge, is roughly $10 x 100 x 0.005, or about $5 across the whole session. Now add a $5 Perfect Pairs side bet on every hand, at a house edge in the middle of its typical range, say 6%. That side bet alone carries an expected loss of roughly $5 x 100 x 0.06, or about $30 — six times your entire main-hand expected loss, from a wager that's only half the size of your main bet. The side bet isn't a small add-on to your session's math, it's usually the dominant source of your expected loss once you add it up.

Why this matters: a side bet's small stake size hides how much house edge it's actually carrying. Comparing dollar amounts wagered makes a $5 side bet look minor next to a $10 main hand — comparing expected loss tells the real story, and the side bet usually loses.

Why casinos push side bets so hard

Side bets exist because they're a highly efficient way for a casino to raise its overall hold on a blackjack table without touching the main game's advertised, well-known low house edge — a number sharp players specifically look for when choosing where to play. A table can keep the same 3:2 blackjack payout and standard rules that make its main game competitive, while still meaningfully improving the table's average revenue per hand through side-bet volume from players who don't separate the two wagers' math in their head. That's also why side bets are marketed with their best-case payout front and center (a 25 to 1 perfect pair, a 100 to 1 suited trips) rather than their actual hit frequency or house edge, which casinos generally aren't required to display prominently the way a slot's RTP sometimes is.

Is a side bet ever worth making?

For most recreational play, no — the math above is the whole argument. There's one narrow exception worth knowing about, purely as a matter of how the game works rather than as encouragement: card counters occasionally track side-bet-specific counts (an "ace-neutral" or dedicated side count) because certain side bets can briefly swing toward the player when a shoe is unusually rich in the specific ranks or suits that side bet rewards. In practice this is a niche, advanced technique with a thin edge even when it exists, casinos actively watch for exactly this kind of pattern, and it has no relevance to how a typical player should treat these bets. For the overwhelming majority of blackjack play, the side bet is a straightforward -EV wager layered on top of a game that, played correctly, is one of the fairest bets on the floor. Frequently asked questions

Do side bets affect how I should play my main blackjack hand?

No. The side bet settles immediately based on your first two cards (and the dealer's up card, for 21+3) and has no bearing on the correct basic-strategy decision for your main hand, which should be played exactly the same way with or without a side bet on the table.

Why do Perfect Pairs paytables vary so much between casinos?

Operators choose their own payout structure for mixed, colored, and perfect pairs, and a more generous-looking top payout on one table can still come with a worse overall house edge than a more modest paytable elsewhere, depending on how the middle tiers are priced.

Is 21+3 better or worse than Perfect Pairs?

Neither is consistently better — both typically land in a similar mid-single-digit-to-high-single-digit house edge range, and the exact number depends entirely on the specific paytable a given casino or online table is running, so it's worth comparing rather than assuming.

Can I win money long-term on blackjack side bets?

Not through ordinary play. Like any negative-expectation bet, individual sessions can produce real wins, especially given how top-heavy the payouts are, but the house edge means the long-run average outcome is a loss regardless of short-term results.
